content:
Multiple legal and business groups, along with the U.S. government, this week submitted briefs to the Supreme Court urging the justices to vacate at least part of a civil contempt ruling against Apple in its lawsuit with Epic Games. Details below.

先說明背景

In late June, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to review Apple's argument over whether a civil contempt ruling against it should be vacated in its lawsuit with Epic Games.

簡單來說，Apple 雖然遵照法庭命令、允許開發者將用戶導向外部購買選項，卻對這些交易收取 27% 佣金。當 Epic 對 Apple 的執行方式提出質疑時，地方法院裁定 Apple 構成民事藐視法庭。

Apple has, from the start, allowed developers to link to external purchase options without paying a commission.

Apple 此後一直嘗試推翻該裁決，辯稱禁制令的實際條文並無禁止其收取佣金，並指下級法院不當地依賴「禁制令的精神」來裁定公司藐視法庭。

For reference, here's what the original order said:

Last week, Apple formally filed its opening brief with the Supreme Court, again arguing that the contempt ruling should be tossed out because the original injunction didn't explicitly bar the company from collecting a commission on purchases made outside the App Store.

Apple 在陳述書中亦指出，若任由藐視法庭的裁斷成立，日後法院執行禁制令時將增加司法越權的風險，令企業難以確定某項命令實際上禁止哪些行為。

The U.S. government and other groups weigh in

Epic Games' response brief is due November 13, but the Supreme Court this week received amicus briefs from the U.S. Department of Justice, through the Solicitor General's office, as well as from several legal and business groups weighing in on Apple's appeal.

司法部在其法庭之友陳述書中指出，「民事藐視法庭……只有在被告的行為明顯受到禁制令明文條款涵蓋時方屬恰當」，並表示 Apple 決定收取 27% 佣金的情況並不符合此原則。

The brief echoes Apple's argument that civil contempt shouldn't be found where there is a "reasonable doubt" over whether the injunction actually prohibits the conduct, and concludes the Supreme Court should "vacate the contempt finding as it relates to the 27% commission."

However, in the same brief, the DOJ said the lower court was correct to find Apple in contempt over its "button design" restrictions, since the injunction clearly required Apple to allow both buttons and links — but Apple's implementation effectively only allowed links.

As for the rest of the disputes — like the various restrictions on where external purchase links could appear — the DOJ said the Supreme Court should set aside the existing ruling and send it back to the lower court to reconsider under the "reasonable doubt" standard.

Beyond the DOJ, the Supreme Court also received amicus briefs from the following groups:

  • U.S. Chamber of Commerce
  • Chamber of Progress
  • Former Federal Antitrust Enforcers
  • International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE)
  • Computer & Communications Industry Association, NetChoice, and the Software & Information Industry Association
  • Washington Legal Foundation (WLF)

Broadly, all of them back a single overarching argument: that Apple cannot properly be held in civil contempt for conduct that wasn't explicitly prohibited by the injunction — and that courts should enforce injunctions based on their actual terms, not their perceived "spirit."

ICLE adds that "choosing a profitable way to comply is still complying"; the former federal antitrust enforcers cite past case law to argue that having a judge decide how much commission Apple can charge "is exactly the kind of 'direct price regulation' that antitrust courts typically shy away from."

Currently, the district court is proceeding with a process to determine how much commission (if any) Apple can collect on outbound purchases, while the Supreme Court reviews the contempt ruling itself.
